name: Aisha Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk at Kestrel Supplies by 7:45, before the warehouse trucks get going. I buy paper, toner, bin liners and cleaning products from about sixty suppliers, and most of my day is phone calls, a big spreadsheet and chasing late deliveries. I like it when I land a good price and the schools I'm buying for don't run out of anything. What wears me out is the shouting when a pallet doesn't turn up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's at home waiting for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tunde drives a city bus, and we've got Noor, who's eleven, and Samir, who's eight. We have a mortgage on a small terraced house, so I do the school run on my way in and he does pickup. I'm still the junior in our buying office, even at 43, because I came into the job late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hype and the bosses will find something else to blame costs on. At work I'd tell Marta in accounts that we've heard this before with the barcode scanners and the new ordering portal. Online I'd probably say nothing, because I don't trust what I post to stay private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, between us, I'd still be worried, and AI has nothing to do with it. Kestrel lost our biggest school customer last spring and they cut my hours by half a day. If a little reorder emailing goes to software, that's the bit they gave me to learn on, so even a small change lands on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and keep my head down. I'd put more into the union fund that Tunde's depot runs, and I'd stop the Saturday takeaway. I'd ask Denise, our senior buyer, to give me the supplier calls rather than the paperwork, because the calls are where a person is needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a held breath. Not a panic, just the mortgage letter on the fridge and the same worry I had last Tuesday. I'm tired of being the person who has to be grateful to have the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm already had a rough year. What exactly happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer left over a price, they said. A big online seller undercut us by a few pence a ream, and nobody upstairs fought for the account. So I trust my bosses to chase cheap numbers, not to look after people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a bit of routine work moved to software, who in your office would notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would notice first, because the invoice matching is half her day. Then me, because my reorders are routine. Denise would be fine, she has twenty years and the supplier relationships. I'd say the juniors always pay first.

say: I'd tell colleagues this is **hype** and we've heard it before.
I'd say the real problem is bosses chasing cheap prices, not technology.
think: Even a small change lands on me, because I'm the **junior** with the routine reorders.
The firm is already squeezed, and AI is not what worries me most.
do: Keep going and keep my head down at work.
Put more into the **union fund** and drop the Saturday takeaway.
Ask Denise for supplier calls instead of the paperwork.
feel: Like holding my breath, with the **mortgage** letter on the fridge.
S0.quote: I'm tired of being the person who has to be grateful to have the job.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **firm's money**, not AI; the lost school account is the real fear.
Distrusts managers more than the technology, and says so with a dry humour.

steps.text: Keep buying stationery and cleaning stock for Kestrel as normal
Skip the Saturday takeaway and put that money in savings
Pay an extra tenner a month into the depot union fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a cover for cutting jobs. At work I'd say what the office manager wants to hear, but at the union meeting I'd say software is doing the buying while pay stays flat. Online I'd say it's the owners who benefit and the rest of us who retrain on our own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the reorder work and the price checking go first, and that's about two thirds of my week. Our buying office has four people and I can see it being two. I'm the newest and I'm the one who never touches the new ordering tools, so you can guess who's number three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union rep for a meeting before anything is announced. I'd keep my savings, about three months, untouched and look at evening classes in logistics, though I hate screens. In the first year I'd apply for supplier-facing jobs, like account manager at a warehouse where people still talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair, like the rules changed halfway through a game I came late to. I get angry first and frightened second, usually in the car park before I go in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors pay first. Who decides that, in your office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decision comes from above, from the finance director, who has a spreadsheet and never meets a school secretary. Denise would argue for us, but she's got her own mortgage. So I'd say juniors pay first because nobody important is standing next to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Tunde the night they told you the reorders were moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tunde straight: we have three months, we cut the phone contract, and we ask my mum to watch the kids if I take evening shifts. He'd say the bus company might cut routes in time too, and we'd just sit there. We've never had both of us at risk before.

say: I'd say this is a **cover for cutting jobs** while pay stays flat.
I'd push the union to demand a say before anything is announced.
think: Reorders and price checks are about **two thirds** of my week, so I'm exposed.
Our buying office of four could become two, and I'm the newest.
do: Ask the **union rep** for a meeting before any announcement.
Look at evening classes in logistics and apply for supplier-facing jobs.
Keep my three months of savings untouched.
feel: Angry first, then frightened, usually in the **car park** before work.
S1.quote: I'd say juniors pay first because nobody important is standing next to us.
fieldNote: Moves quickly from anger at bosses to a practical plan built around the **union**.
Names a concrete number: two thirds of her week is routine buying.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a meeting before anything is announced
Apply for account manager jobs at warehouses with supplier calls
Sign up for an evening logistics course at the local college
Leave the three months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it should never be allowed to happen this fast without rules. At work I'd say nothing, because you don't say that kind of thing to the office manager. In my street WhatsApp group I'd say governments have to slow it down or pay people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished in this job, probably within a year or two of it arriving. Everything I do is thinking work, calls, comparing prices, deciding what to order, and a machine does that for nothing. My partner's bus job is safe a few years longer, but I can't count on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join the union rally and write to my councillor, because I think rules are the only thing that helps. I'd also sell the car we hardly use and cut the kids' swimming club to save about a hundred a month. In the first year I'd look at any hands-on work, warehouse supervisor or a delivery coordinator, because robots take longer there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel like I'm standing on a railway line hearing a train. I can't sleep and I snap at my daughter Noor over homework, then feel awful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently on day one if the warning was only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On day one I'd ask for a meeting with the whole office, not just me, because alone I'd be sacked first. I'd also ask what they'll pay us to leave. Two years is too short to retrain anyone properly, so I'd want the union to bargain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if this really happens that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies and the owners, not the machine. They get the profit, and then the council gets the bill for the people who can't pay their rent. I don't blame myself, though I know I'll act like I do.

say: I'd say governments must **slow it down** or pay people.
I'd stay quiet at work and speak up at the union rally.
think: Everything I do is **thinking work**, so I'd expect to lose this job within a year or two.
Tunde's bus job lasts longer, but we can't rely on one wage.
do: Join the **rally** and write to my councillor.
Sell the spare car and cut the swimming club, saving about a hundred a month.
Look for hands-on roles like warehouse supervisor.
feel: Like standing on a railway line hearing a train, **sleepless** and snappy.
S2.quote: I feel like I'm standing on a railway line hearing a train. I can't sleep and I snap at my daughter Noor over homework, then feel awful about it.
fieldNote: Blames **owners** and tech firms rather than the machine; politics and union come first.
Sees the 3-year robot gap as her only escape route into hands-on work.

steps.text: Write to my councillor and go to the union rally
Ask for a whole-office meeting about redundancy terms
Sell the spare car and cut the kids' swimming club
Apply for warehouse supervisor or delivery coordinator jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a fighting chance if people act now. At work I'd say we should ask management for a plan. With friends I'd say the unions have to get a deal before it gets here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still scared, but I think I could get out in time. I'm 43, so by 2031 I'd be 48 and the kids would be at secondary school. If I move into something with hands in it, I might get through to 2034 before the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd retrain, even though I hate it, probably a warehouse supervisor certificate or a transport planning course, one evening a week. I'd pay the mortgage down faster by cutting holidays, and I'd ask Tunde to go for the driver-trainer role at his depot. In the first year after it arrives I'd already be out of buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels shaky but not hopeless. Five years lets me be angry and busy at the same time, which is better than just angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a different kind of clock. What does it let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mummy's job is changing because computers are getting very clever, and we're going to be careful with money for a while. Noor would ask a hundred questions and Samir would ask if we still get pizza on Friday. I'd say yes, but smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain to Noor and Samir what's going on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me learn slowly and keep my pride. Two years would mean begging for any job. With five I can choose a job I might even like, and keep paying for Noor's school trips.

say: I'd say five years is a **fighting chance** if we act now.
I'd press management for a written plan.
think: I'm still scared, but I might get out in time and into **hands-on work**.
By 2031 I'd be 48 with the kids at secondary school.
do: Retrain one evening a week for a **warehouse supervisor** certificate.
Cut holidays to pay the mortgage down faster.
Ask Tunde to go for the driver-trainer role at his depot.
feel: **Shaky but not hopeless**; being angry and busy is better than just angry.
S3.quote: Five years lets me learn slowly and keep my pride. Two years would mean begging for any job.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her anger into a **plan**; the gap before robots is central.
Keeps the family in view, including how she would explain it to the children.

steps.text: Start a warehouse supervisor certificate one evening a week
Skip the summer holiday and pay the mortgage down
Ask Tunde to apply for the driver-trainer role
Move into a supplier-facing job outside buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for governments to get their act together, and they'd better. At work I'd carry on as usual and tell people not to panic. Online I'd back anyone calling for a public fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years almost feels safe, because Noor will be 21 and Samir 18 and my mortgage might be nearly paid. I'd still worry about what the world looks like for them, not me. But I know a decade goes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and watch carefully. I'd go on paying the union fund and ask Denise to teach me the supplier side properly, since that's where a person still matters. In the first year I'd save a bit more and take one evening course, but I wouldn't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels almost calm, with a little guilt. I know it's the same destination, but it's easier to look at when you can see your daughter finish school first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes about how you feel today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years changes how I feel but not what I'd tell my bosses. I'd still want a written promise about what happens to staff. Time to adjust is only a gift if somebody uses it, and I don't trust them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2030 I'd want the mortgage cut down, a qualification in my bag, and a union that has a deal for people like me. Mostly I'd want Noor and Samir to have more choices than I had, with a better education than my secondary school.

say: I'd tell people a decade is **plenty of time** and not to panic.
I'd back calls for a public fund.
think: Ten years almost feels safe, since the kids will be grown and the **mortgage** nearly paid.
I'd still worry what kind of world they inherit.
do: Ask Denise to teach me the **supplier side** properly.
Take one evening course, without rushing.
Save a little more each month.
feel: Almost **calm**, with a little guilt about it.
S4.quote: Time to adjust is only a gift if somebody uses it, and I don't trust them to.
fieldNote: The longer horizon relaxes her, but her **distrust** of employers does not move.
Thinks about the children's choices more than her own job, which is the clearest sign of her priorities.

steps.text: Keep buying for Kestrel and watch the market closely
Ask Denise to teach me the supplier relationship side
Add fifty pounds a month to the mortgage overpayment
Take one evening course in procurement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It leaves no time for Noor and Samir's life to settle, and no time for any rules. I'd rather the people who built these machines worry about my mortgage than have me do it alone. What would help is a written promise from the firm, a union deal on redundancy and retraining pay, and something like a public fund for people who lose work overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I like about my job. I like finding the stock a school really needs at a fair price. It would be a pity if nobody saw that as a skill, even if I'm only the junior.

headlineQuote: I'd rather the people who built these machines worry about my mortgage than have me do it alone.
portrait: Aisha, 43, is a **junior buyer** at Kestrel Supplies, married to a bus driver, with two children and a mortgage.
She distrusts bosses more than technology and turns to her **union** and politics first.
She never uses AI tools, so she expects to be cut early because the work is routine desk work.
Her plan is practical: save, retrain in logistics, and move toward hands-on jobs where robots arrive later.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because there is no time for rules or retraining.
whatWouldHelp: A written staff **promise**, union deal on redundancy, and a public fund for people who lose work fast.
